Subject: Scheduling challenge for a multi‑mode, resource‑constrained project

Overview
We are preparing the integrated schedule for a project that consists of multiple interdependent activities. Each activity can be executed in more than one way, offering tradeoffs between speed, resource consumption, and cost. Our task is to select an execution approach for each activity and sequence the work to meet all timing and dependency requirements while finishing the project as quickly as possible within a fixed budget.

Execution modes and tradeoffs
- Each activity has multiple execution modes. Faster options reduce duration but typically consume more resources and cost more; slower options are less resource‑intensive and cheaper but take longer.
- Exactly one mode must be chosen for each activity. Once an activity starts, it runs to completion without interruption.
- Resources are renewable: capacity is consumed only while an activity is in progress and is released as soon as the activity finishes.

Dependencies and timing constraints
- Precedence relationships define which activities must finish before successors can begin.
- Some dependencies include minimum waits (the successor must start no sooner than a set time after the predecessor finishes) and some also impose maximum waits (the successor must start within a specified time window after the predecessor finishes).
- Certain activities have earliest allowed start times (release dates), and a subset have hard deadlines that must be met.

Resource limits and the conservative safety rule
- The project uses multiple renewable resource types, each with a fixed capacity. While activities run, they consume units of these resources according to their chosen modes.
- To protect against overload under uncertainty in mode selection, we apply a conservative safety rule for activities that are not connected by precedence:
  • If there exists at least one pair of modes (one per activity) and at least one resource for which the combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, those two activities may not overlap. They must be sequenced so that one finishes before the other starts.  
  • This rule is enforced pairwise across unrelated activity pairs. It is the only resource constraint; there is no separate, continuous “at all times” capacity check beyond these sequencing decisions.
- This approach means that even if some mode combinations for two activities would fit simultaneously, the possibility of overload in any combination requires us to order them.

Budget constraint
- The project has a fixed total budget that caps the sum of the chosen mode costs across all activities. This is a non‑renewable constraint at the project level; we must plan mode selections to stay within the cap while meeting timing needs.

Scheduling goal
Our goal is to:
- Choose a mode for each activity
- Sequence activities to respect all precedence relations, minimum and maximum delays, release dates, and deadlines
- Apply the conservative pairwise safety rule for resources
- Complete the entire project as early as possible while keeping total mode costs within the budget

Implications for planning
- The primary tradeoff is between speed and cost at the activity level, balanced against global budget limits.
- Conservative resource sequencing may force additional ordering between otherwise independent tasks, influencing both mode choices and start times.
- Release dates, deadlines, and maximum delay limits can compress feasible windows, requiring careful coordination across dependencies.
